## **Notes** 

###### Units used: 

Unless otherwise stated, all statistics on platinum and palladium supply and demand are expressed in terms of fine metal content.  All references in this publication to “ounces” refer to troy ounces. 

**One troy ounce =** 31.103 grammes **One tonne =** 32,151 troy ounces **“dollar”** US dollar unless otherwise stated 

###### Prices: 

Unless otherwise stated, US dollars and their equivalents are for the pm fixes of the London Platinum and Palladium Market. 

Terminology: 

Estimates of **supply** _include_ mine production and the recycling of both scrapped autocatalysts and old jewellery but _exclude_ contributions from above-ground stocks, such as supplies from stocks controlled by state institutions in Russia. 

**Demand** estimates are _net_ of recycling with the exception of autocatalyst and jewellery, where _gross_ demand is shown. i.e. the total amount of metal supplied to these two sectors.  Estimates of recycling from scrapped autocatalysts and jewellery are shown separately as part of supply given their scale and potential for change.  (This year’s survey is the second in which we have presented jewellery fabrication as gross with a separate series for scrap; prior to this, jewellery was shown on a net basis.)  Estimates of demand exclude the movements of any above-ground stocks held within the specified industries, for example any changes in stocks held by the automotive industry. 

By simple arithmetic, this leaves either a **“Gross Surplus or Deficit”** before any movements in above-ground stocks are considered.  This is a critical measure of the underlying fundamentals of platinum and palladium and indicates the extent to which fabrication demand may have depended on the release of above-ground stocks, o

r otherwise.  At the same time, this also indicates the change in global above-ground stocks. 

Unless otherwise stated, all references to **“above-ground stocks”** of platinum and palladium refer to stocks of refined metal, of a form and quality accepted as good delivery in the Zurich market and the world’s principal commodity exchanges.  Our supply/demand tables also show **“Estimated Movements in Stocks”** .  These specific movements relate only to above-ground stock holdings for which reasonable estimates of movement can be made and attributed. A listing and breakdown of these appears in the more detailed tables in the Appendices section of this Survey. 

Having allowed for the Estimated Movements in Stocks as defined above, the **“Residual Surplus or Deficit”** is arrived at by deduction.  A **residual deficit** implies the extent to which **_other above-ground stocks_** , including those held by financial institutions and/or investors, were released to meet fabrication demand.  Conversely a **residual surplus** implies the extent to which these **_other above-ground stock_** holdings were added to.  However, this should not be construed as indicating the change in global above-ground stocks.  For this, please refer to the reported Gross Surplus or Deficit. 

**Throughout the tables, totals may not add due to independent rounding.**

### **1. Executive Summary** 

###### **Introduction & Prices** 

_In terms of recent events in Japan, this would seem to have already had a dramatic impact on PGM prices (as well as across the rest of the precious metals complex), as investors reacted quickly to the bearing this disaster could have on the supply/demand balance for each metal.  It is inconceivable that Japanese demand in autocatalyst and industrial applications will not be adversely affected, although it is far too early to comment on the likely extent of this.  As a result, both the price outlook and supply/demand forecasts contained in this report represent the situation as we saw it before these tragic events unfolded.  To the best of our ability, we will therefore attempt to assess the impact of this disaster in our next report._ 

Having regained traction over the last quarter of 2010, platinum and palladium prices have since posted further gains in the early part of 2011 in conjunction with a weakening dollar, rising oil prices and the unfolding drama in North Africa and the Middle East. Undoubtedly, the principal driver of these gains has again been investment flows, with long positioning in futures and exchange traded funds having increased considerably over the three months to the end of February.  Overall, investors increased their exposure during this period by some 0.7M ounces of platinum and over 0.5M ounces of palladium, raising their already elevated stakes by some 23% and 15% respectively since the end of November. 

Thi

s confirms resoundingly that the case for investment in precious metals – and gold in particular – is still very much intact, with recent geopolitical tensions adding a new dimension to the established mix of incentives. Monetary policy (especially in the United States) remains exceptionally loose, cultivating long standing concerns over dollar debasement and the risk of high inflation in future. The sovereign debt crisis in Europe – although out of the headlines for now – continues to resonate; ensuring lingering doubts over the banking system, economic growth and the long term viability of the euro project. Meanwhile, interest rates in the world’s developed economies remain at or close to zero and are generally negative in real terms. Consequently, with cash being a non-returning asset, the opportunity cost of investing in precious metals is exceptionally low, while the desire for capital gains from alternate investments (including safe-haven assets) remains high. Notwithstanding the outcome of the current tensions in North Africa and the Middle East, we remain of the view that conditions for precious metals investment will remain conducive for some time to come. While the sovereign debt crisis in Europe appears to have been contained for now, the spectre of this indebtedness remains very real and has resulted in aggressive action by many European countries to cut their budget deficits. Meanwhile, the United States continues to run huge fiscal deficits, financed in part through the Fed’s quantitative easing programme and there is a risk that the perilous state of US finances may yet cause a transAtlantic shift in the focus of sovereign debt concerns. However, as things stand, it seems unlikely that the Fed will attempt any roll-back of monetary policy before the latter part of 2012 at the earliest. Therefore, we expect that initial actions on this front will include only gentle upward movements in interest rates for fear of derailing the recovery. Overall, these circumstances signal further dollar weakness over the intervening period and an extended run of favourable investment conditions for precious metals (at least in dollar terms). We e

xpect these conditions to remain firmly in place throughout 2011 and 2012, before weakness begins to emerge during 2013. 

As a result, our stance on gold prices remains positive (especially so in 2011 and 2012) and we believe this will form a favourable investment climate for platinum and palladium as well.  In the case of **platinum prices** , after its annual average hit a record high of $1,611 in 2010 (33% up on its average in 2009), we predict an average of $1,855 in 2011 and a marginally lower $1,820 in 2012.  Thereafter, as clouds begin to gather over the broader case for precious metals investment, we anticipate some weakening in 2013, with platinum prices easing to an average in that year of $1,695. However, with platinum’s underlying fundamentals remaining less than supportive, this profile of elevated prices is predicated on the idea of continuing investor support, without which platinum prices would be in some jeopardy.  Over the forecast period, we expect a continuing gross surplus for platinum, with this remaining especially large in 2011 and 2012 (broadly similar to 2010 levels), before easing in 2013. 

The major causes of this continuing gross surplus are relatively subdued demand growth in autocatalyst applications, alongside supply growth from mine production and recycling.  With a recurring gross surplus, above-ground stocks of platinum will continue to rise over the forecast period, building on substantial 

increases in 2009 (a large gross surplus and substantial industry de-stocking) and 2010.  This leads to a level of platinum stock at the end of 2013 which appears worryingly large, given our expectation that investor sentiment is likely to be weakening around that time. 

While our forecast of elevated dollar prices for platinum may not translate fully into higher prices for producers in South Africa, these should (together with robust palladium prices) support a moderate recovery in platinum mine production, which turned the corner in 2010 after three years of decline.  Furthermore, these prices are not expected to deter demand for platinum jewellery fabrication, as we anticipate sufficient volatility to enable demand from China to improve over the forecast period (although moderately in 2011), after a set-back last year. 

In 2010, **palladium prices** finished the year at $791, with the annual average weighing in at $527; double the average of 2009.   This was palladium’s best performance since 2001 when the intra-year price spiked to $1,100 in January – a level we expect palladium to revisit in 2013 and perhaps as early as 2012.  We predict average prices for palladium of $875 in 2011 and $1,020 in 2012, before a further move higher in 2013 when we anticipate an average price of $1,100.  In addition to resilient investor interest and the anticipated conclusion of Russian government sales, the case for higher palladium prices is supported by the return of a sizeable gross defcit in 2010, which is expected to increase o

As we indicated in our previous report in December, the weight of anecdotal evidence, together with our own modelling of this situation, signal the likelihood that sales from these stockpiles of palladium will in all probability draw to a close within the horizon of this forecast. After significant liquidations estimated at 0.9M ounces in 2010, we expect sales to continue at similar levels in 2011. However, whilst we believe that 2011 is most likely the final year in which elevated sales will occur, we feel it is prudent to allow for some residual sales (although sharply reduced) in 2012 and to a lesser extent in 2013, as this programme finally draws to a close. When Russian government sales and last year’s substantial ETF inflows are included, palladium registered a substantial residual defcit in 2010; its’ first since 2000. Over the forecast period, further residual deficits are expected, even though ETF inflows are expected to subside, while Russian government sales continue (although with marked reductions from 2012). The emergence of a residual deficit from 2010 – the first in ten years – is a significant development and further supports the increasingly positive sentiment which has surrounded palladium over the last year or more. However, while these residual deficits (and their associated gross deficits in particular) enhance the interest of investors, they also indicate that net disinvestment in palladium has already occurred in 2010 (by implication, from OTC investors) and will need to continue over the forecast period to redress the shortfall between new supply and fabrication demand. For this to occur, prices will need to be sufficiently attractive to induce the required amount of net selling from investors – especially so in 2013 when Russian government sales are expected to be all but over. ###### **Market balances & above-ground stocks** In 2010, we estimate that **platinum** registered a further substantial gross surplus of more than 0.9M ounces; an upward revision since our previous report due mainly to increased mine production. This was the fifth year in a row where significant gross surplus occurred, with these having escalated since 2009. As a reminder, these gross surpluses represent the underlying balance between new supply (mine production and recycling) and fabrication demand across all applications. By definition, this excludes allocations to ETFs and the effect of other movements in pre-existing above-ground stocks (such as industry de-stocking which occurred in 2009). Together with the scale of above-ground stocks, the levels of gross surplus (or deficit) remain our preferred measure of the underlying health of the market. (Note: our estimates for above-ground stocks include allocations in ETFs). Looking forward, we expect a continuation of these circumstances in 2011 and 2012, with an underlying gross surplus in the region of 1M ounces of platinum in each of those years. This is not expected to ease materially until 2013, when demand growth finally outpaces the increase in supply, to produce a reduced gross surplus of a little less than 0.7M ounces. (Overall, these estimates are higher than previously indicated, based on a mix of upward revisions to supply and some downward revisions in demand, chiefly in autocatalyst and jewellery). Inevitably, these projected gross surpluses will feed through to above- ground platinum stocks, inflating them still further over the forecast period. With stocks at the end of 2010 having swollen already to an estimated 3.9M ounces of platinum (the result of five years of gross surplus and industry de-stocking in 2009), we forecast these will rise to a total of 6.5M ounces by the end of 2013; the equivalent of around ten months fabrication demand at that time. Ultimately, this inflation in above-ground stocks is a millstone around platinum’s neck which will weigh increasingly on prices once the currently positive climate for investment eventually weakens. Meanwhile, as we await that development, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that with prices expected to remain elevated, investors will continue to reward the mining industry for producing significant amounts of platinum for which there is no immediate fabrication demand. While clearly unsustainable over the longer term, the pay-back for this will most likely be deferred until after the horizon of this forecast. ###### **Demand** 

In the **platinum** market, total demand over 20112013 is expected to see a period of uninterrupted gains.  Following a somewhat muted recovery of around 5% last year, 2011 is expected to realise a 3% increase.  Thereafter, growth averages 6% in 2012 and 2013, boosted primarily by healthy Chinese jewellery demand.  Nonetheless, offtake of 7.76M ounces in the final year of the forecast still remains below that of the pre-crisis level of 7.93M ounces (seen in 2007).  Since the December report, the forecast series has been revised lower, due mostly to downwards revisions to the outlook for autocatalyst demand, as well as a trimmed jewellery series. 

The outlook for the **autocatalyst** sector over the next two years remains generally lacklustre, with 2013 then seeing a more significant improvement.  After a revival of 11% in 2010, thanks largely to various government incentive schemes that stimulated auto sales, their absence this year contributes to a more modest 3% rise.  This improves to 4% and 8% in 2012 and 2013 respectively, resulting in offtake of 3.36M ounces in 2013, although this still falls short of 2007’s record high of 4.07M ounces. 

The underlying reasons behind this growth profile remain unchanged from the last report.  First, the 

main thrust of the recovery in vehicle production will take place in the gasoline, and therefore palladiumrich, markets, namely China as well as other emerging areas.  Moreover, platinum receives less support from Europe’s auto sector, the largest market for platinum autocatalyst demand, as th

e light diesel sector here is rapidly approaching maturity. Second, platinum faces ongoing competition from palladium within the diesel sector, its traditional stronghold, with palladium forecast to make further substitution gains to the detriment of its sister metal. Compared to the December report, autocatalyst demand has been revised lower in each year of the forecast, with the reductions concentrated in China. In terms of platinum **jewellery** , the demand profile is set to show three years of increasingly healthy gains, following a price-related drop of 11% in 2010. This year, offtake rises by 5%, and improves thereafter to 9% and 10% in 2012 and 2013 respectively. The declining price profile at this time produces a robust (and positive) response from China and this, combined with modest gains in North America and Europe, are more than sufficient to overcome weakness in Japan. The forecast series has been adjusted marginally lower since the previous report. Last year, **total palladium** demand rebounded by some 13% to reach 8.58M ounces. This surpassed the previous record of 8.40M ounces (reached in 2007), and forms the base from which three further years of gains are expected to emerge. Although the rate of growth will slow somewhat (averaging a still respectable 5% per annum), we expect demand in 2013 to near 9.80M ounces, driven by growth in the autocatalyst and electronics sectors. Palladium is set to find support from both the gasoline and diesel auto sectors. In the former, this will come from robust growth in a number of emerging markets, which favour palladium-dominant gasoline vehicles over diesel; whilst in the latter, palladium is set to make further substitution inroads, at platinum’s expense. The forecast has been adjusted lower compared to the December forecast. The forecast for palladium **jewellery** , in contrast, is one of falling demand through to 2013 (the series has also been revised lower since the previous report). We expect to see three years of consecutive declines, which take demand by the end of the forecast to just 605,000 ounces, less than half the peak reached in 2005. The weaker trend will largely be driven by h

eavy losses in China, as support at the retail level for carat palladium jewellery declines sharply, the product of ongoing VAT issues, a lack of price transparency and low consumer awareness. 

With regards to **industrial demand** , the outlook for platinum and palladium offtake remains almost unchanged since the last forecast.  Platinum industrial fabrication will remain broadly unchanged this year, followed by growth of some 8% in 2012, thanks largely to expansions in the glass and petroleum sectors.  In 2013, demand dips slightly, although this will mostly be due to the comparison against a strong 2012. Palladium industrial demand, meanwhile, is set to achieve modest gains over the next two years, followed by a flat outcome in 2013.  The most substantial change to palladium has centred on the electronics forecast, which has been adjusted lower across the entire forecast. 

Turning to **retail investment** , the forecast series for platinum has been raised marginally from the December report, while palladium’s profile has remained unchanged.  Platinum investment is set to decline throughout the 2011-13 period, as investor interest wanes.  In contrast, palladium’s more supportive supply/demand fundamentals may attract additional investment, but the volumes are expected to be modest.  As a result, total retail investment in palladium is forecast to remain little changed through to 2013. 

###### **Supply** 

**Total platinum supply** is expected to post successive gains over the next three years to a record high of 8.44M ounces in 2013.  Each major area of supply will contribute to this outcome although the most significant gains will come from mine production, followed by autocatalyst supply.  Taking each in turn, mine supply is expected to grow by 410,000 ounces, comparing the totals for 2010 and 2013, with the most noteworthy gains achieved by South Africa and Canada over this period.
